newsitem.title: USA: U.S. makes new offer on global financial services.
newsitem.headline: U.S. makes new offer on global financial services.

text.p: The United States on Monday made a new conditional offer to the World Trade Organization to try to spur stalled talks on a pact to liberalize financial services trade.

Washington is offering "substantially full market access and national treatment to foreign banking, securities and insurance service suppliers" in the United States, a joint statement by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said.
But it specifies that trade partners must respond with a more generous offer for U.S. firms to operate abroad.

"To make this offer permanent by the December 1997 negotiating deadline, it is critical that our trading partners, especially the key emerging markets, submit significantly improved offers that establish a level playing field for U.S. firms to compete effectively," the statement said.

Rubin and Barshefsky said the United States was "fully committed to reaching a successful conclusion to the WTO negotiations" and emphasized the improved access that was being offered to foreign firms in the huge U.S. market.

They said the United States was prepared to lock in a Most Favored Nation (MFN) commitment to the U.S. financial market and to make sure that foreign participants get the benefit of expected U.S. banking reforms.
In addition, state residency and citizenship requirements for foreign insurers operating in the United States will be removed, Rubin and Barshefsky said.
In return, the United States wants specific commitments in the form of offers from WTO trade partners to make sure that U.S. firms are able compete more freely overseas.

"These offers should permit U.S. firms to establish as a branch or to incorporate without ownership restrictions, and to fully participate throughout the market on the basis of national treatment," the statement said.

In some case, the United States would be prepared to consider phased-in commitments from foreign trade partners. This was likely a reference to developing countries fearful their industries might be overwhelmed by U.S. competition.

The Clinton administration, seeking to open up global trade in insurance, banking, securities and other financial services, is consulting extensively with U.S. businesses which in turn are in contact with their foreign counterparts, the statement said.
